Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 108, verses 1–3:

It is Meccan according to Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Kalbi and Muqatil, and Medinan according to al-Hasan, ʿIkrimah, Mujahid and Qatadah.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn al-Zubayr and ʿAʾishah that the surah of al-Kawthar was revealed in Mecca.

In the name of Allah, the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful.

The majority of readers recite ﴿Innā aʿṭaynāka﴾ (﴿Indeed, We have given you﴾). al-Hasan, Ibn Muḥaysin, Ṭalḥah and al-Zaʿfarānī read ﴿Anṭaynāka﴾ with an *nūn* (﴿Indeed, We have given you﴾, with the verb written with the letter *nūn*).

It is said that this is the dialect of the pure Arabs (*al-ʿarabiyyah al-ʿāribah*).

al-Aʿshā said:

*"Your gifts are the finest gifts of kings; you protect what is lawful and give away the unlawful."*

The word ﴿al-Kawthar﴾ is of the pattern *fawʿal*, derived from *al-kathrah* (abundance). It is used as an attribute to express intensity in abundance, like *al-nawfal* from *al-nafl* and *al-jawhar* from *al-jahr*.

The Arabs call everything abundant in number, quantity or worth *kawthar*. From this is the saying of the poet:

*"The dust of death has risen until it has become abundant."*

According to this, the meaning is: Indeed, We have given you, O Muhammad, abundant good that has reached the utmost extent of abundance.

Most of the exegetes, as al-Wahidi reported, held that al-Kawthar is a river in Paradise. It is also said that it is the Pool (*ḥawḍ*) of the Prophet (ﷺ) on the Standing Place (on the Day of Judgment). This was said by ʿAṭāʾ.

ʿIkrimah said: al-Kawthar is prophethood.

al-Hasan said: it is the Qur'an.

al-Hasan ibn al-Fadl said: it is the interpretation of the Qur'an and the lightening of the laws.

Abu Bakr ibn ʿAyyash said: it is the great number of companions and of the community (*ummah*).

Ibn Kaysan said: it is generosity (*al-īthār*).

It is also said that it is Islam, that it is the elevation of mention, that it is the light of the heart, that it is intercession, that it is miracles, that it is the answering of supplication, that it is "There is no god but Allah," that it is understanding of the religion, and that it is the five daily prayers. The correct view will be explained later.

﴿So pray to your Lord﴾. The *fāʾ* indicates that what follows is a consequence of what precedes. The intended meaning is a command to him (ﷺ) to persist in establishing the obligatory prayers. ﴿And sacrifice﴾ the camels, which were the best of the wealth of the Arabs.

Muhammad ibn Kaʿb said: some people used to pray to other than Allah and sacrifice to other than Allah, so Allah commanded His Prophet (ﷺ) that his prayer and his sacrifice be for Him alone.

Qatadah, ʿAṭāʾ and ʿIkrimah said: the intended meaning is the ʿEid prayer and the sacrifice of the Udhiyah (festival sacrifice).

It was said regarding *al-naḥr* (sacrifice, or the chest): placing the right hand upon the left during prayer, opposite the chest (*naḥr*). This was said by Muhammad ibn Kaʿb.

It is also said: it is raising the hands in prayer at the takbir up to the level opposite the chest.

It is also said: it is facing the qiblah with one's chest. This was said by al-Farrāʾ, al-Kalbi and Abu al-Aḥwas.

al-Farrāʾ said: I heard some Arabs say *nataḥāwar*, meaning *natagābal* (we face one another): the chest of this one facing the chest of that one, i.e., opposite it. From this is the saying of the poet:

*"O Abu Ḥakam, you are not a man of contention in your life, and the master of the people of al-Abṭaḥ is the one who faces (others)."*

That is, *al-mutaḥāwir* means the one who faces (another).

Ibn al-Aʿrabi said: it is a man standing in prayer facing the *miḥrāb*, from their saying: "Their dwellings face one another (*tatanāḥar*)," meaning they face one another.

It is reported from ʿAṭāʾ that he said: He was commanded to sit upright between the two prostrations until his chest is visible.

Sulayman al-Taymi said: the meaning is: raise your hands in supplication to your chest. The apparent meaning of the verse is a command to him (ﷺ) concerning prayer in general and sacrifice in general, and that he should make both of them for Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and not for anyone else. (p-1660) What the Sunnah has stated as an explanation of this general command, by a specific type, is in the status of a restriction of it, and it will come, Allah willing.

﴿Indeed, your enemy is the one cut off﴾. That is: indeed, your hater is the one cut off from good in general, so that it includes the good of this world and the Hereafter. Or it means: the one who has no offspring. Or: the one whose mention does not remain after his death.

The apparent meaning of the verse is general, and that this is the condition of everyone who hates the Prophet (ﷺ). That the cause of revelation was al-ʿĀs ibn Wāʾil does not contradict this, since what is considered is the generality of the wording, not the specificity of the cause, as has been mentioned before.

It was said: When the males among a man's children died, the people of the Jahiliyyah would say: "So-and-so has been cut off (*buttira*)." When the son of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), Ibrahim, died, Abu Jahl went out to his companions and said: "Muhammad has been cut off," so the verse was revealed. It is also said that the one who said this was ʿUqbah ibn Abi Muʿayṭ. The lexicographers said: *al-abtar* among men is the one who has no son; among animals, the one who has no tail; and every matter whose good effect has been cut off is *abtar*. The root *al-batr* means cutting. It is said: *batartu al-shay batran*, I cut the thing.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ahmad, Abu Dawud, al-Nasaʾi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan reported from Anas, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) dozed off briefly, then he raised his head smiling and said: 'Indeed, a surah was just revealed to me.' Then he recited ﴿Indeed, We have given you al-Kawthar﴾ until he finished it. Then he said: 'Do you know what al-Kawthar is?' They said: 'Allah and His Messenger know best.' He said: 'It is a river which my Lord has given me in Paradise, upon which is abundant good. My community will come to it on the Day of Resurrection. Its vessels are as numerous as the stars. A servant of them will be pulled back, and I will say: "O Lord, he is from my community," and it will be said: "You do not know what he innovated after you."'"

Muslim also reported it in his Ṣaḥīḥ.

al-Bukhari, Muslim and others reported from Anas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "I entered Paradise, and behold, there was a river whose two banks were tents of pearls. I struck with my hand at what the water flows through, and behold, it was musk, extremely fragrant. I said: 'What is this, O Jibril?' He said: 'This is al-Kawthar which Allah has given you.'" It has been reported from Anas through several chains, all of which explicitly state that al-Kawthar is the river that is in Paradise.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, al-Bukhari, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh reported from ʿAʾishah that she was asked about His saying: ﴿Indeed, We have given you al-Kawthar﴾, and she said: "It is a river which was given to your Prophet (ﷺ) in the innermost parts of Paradise (*buṭnān al-jannah*)."

Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn ʿAbbas that it is a river in Paradise.

al-Ṭabarānī in al-Awsaṭ reported from Ḥudhayfah concerning His saying: ﴿Indeed, We have given you al-Kawthar﴾, that he said: "A river in Paradise." al-Suyuti graded its chain as *ḥasan* (good).

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Usamah ibn Zayd, traced back to the Prophet (ﷺ) (*marfūʿan*): "It was said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): 'You have been given a river in Paradise called al-Kawthar.' He said: 'Yes, and its earth is ruby, coral, emerald and pearl.'"

Ibn Mardawayh reported from ʿAmr ibn Shuʿayb, from his father, from his grandfather, that "a man said: 'O Messenger of Allah, what is al-Kawthar?' He said: 'It is a river from the rivers of Paradise which Allah has given me.'" These ḥadīths indicate that al-Kawthar is the river in Paradise, so it is necessary to adopt this and not rely on other explanations. And although the linguistic meaning of al-Kawthar is abundant good in the language of the Arabs, whoever interprets it with something more general than what has been established from the Prophet (ﷺ) is giving an interpretation that looks to the linguistic meaning.

Likewise, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi, who graded it sound (*ṣaḥḥaḥahu*), Ibn Majah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh reported from ʿAṭāʾ ibn al-Sāʾib, who said: Muhārib ibn Dithār said: Saʿid ibn Jubayr said concerning al-Kawthar: "I said: 'Tell us from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said it is the abundant good.' He said: 'He spoke truly, indeed it is abundant good. But Ibn ʿUmar told us that when ﴿Indeed, We have given you al-Kawthar﴾ was revealed, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "al-Kawthar is a river in Paradise, its two banks are of gold, it flows over pearls and rubies, its soil is more fragrant than musk, its water is whiter than milk and sweeter than honey."'"

al-Bukhari, Ibn Jarir and al-Ḥākim, through the route of Abu Bishr from Saʿid ibn Jubayr, from Ibn ʿAbbas, reported that he said concerning al-Kawthar: "It is the good which Allah gave him."

Abu Bishr said: I said to Saʿid ibn Jubayr: "Indeed, some people claim that it is a river in Paradise." He said: "The river that is in Paradise is part of the good which Allah gave him."

This tafsir from the scholar of the Ummah, Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him, looks to the linguistic meaning as we have made known. But the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) has explained it, in what is authentically reported from him, as the river that is in Paradise. And when Allah's river comes, the river of Maʿqil is void.

Ibn Abi Ḥātim, al-Ḥākim, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan reported from ʿAli ibn Abi Ṭalib, who said: "When this surah was revealed upon the Prophet (ﷺ), ﴿Indeed, We have given you al-Kawthar﴾, ﴿So pray to your Lord and sacrifice﴾, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to Jibril: 'What is this *naḥīrah* (sacrifice) which my Lord has commanded me with?' He said: 'It is not a *naḥīrah*, but it commands you, when you begin the prayer with the takbir, to raise your hands when you say the takbir, when you bow, and when you raise your head from bowing. For it is our prayer and the prayer of the angels who are in the seven heavens. Indeed, every thing has an adornment, and the adornment of prayer is raising the hands at every takbir.' The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Raising the hands is from the humbling (*istikānah*) about which Allah said: ﴿So they did not humble themselves before their Lord, nor do they supplicate﴾ [al-Muʾminun: 76].'" This is through the route of Muqatil ibn Ḥayyān from al-Aṣbagh ibn Nubātah from ʿAli.

Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn ʿAbbas concerning the verse, that he said: "Indeed Allah revealed to His Messenger that he should raise his hands opposite his chest when he says the takbir for prayer; that is the *naḥr*."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, al-Bukhari in his History, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Ḥātim, al-Dāraquṭnī in al-Afrād, Abu al-Shaykh, al-Ḥākim, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan reported from ʿAli ibn Abi Ṭalib, concerning His saying: ﴿So pray to your Lord and sacrifice﴾, that he said: "He placed his right hand on the middle of his left forearm, then he placed both of them on his chest in prayer."

Abu al-Shaykh and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan reported from Anas, from the Prophet (ﷺ), something similar.

Ibn Abi Ḥātim, Ibn Shāhīn in his Sunan, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi reported from Ibn ʿAbbas concerning ﴿So pray to your Lord and sacrifice﴾, that he said: "When you pray and raise your head from bowing, stand upright."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Ibn ʿAbbas concerning the verse, that he said: "The obligatory prayer, and the slaughter on the day of al-Aḍḥā (ʿEid al-Adha)."

al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan reported from him concerning ﴿And sacrifice﴾, that he said: "It means: slaughter on the Day of Sacrifice."

al-Bazzār, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Ḥātim and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "Kaʿb ibn al-Ashraf came to Mecca, and the Quraysh said to him: 'You are the best of the people of Medina and their master. Do you not see this *ṣābiʾ* (apostate, one who has left his religion), cut off from his people, who claims he is better than us, while we are the people of the pilgrimage, the people of the watering, and the people of the keys (of the Kaʿbah)?' He said: 'You are better than him.' So ﴿Indeed, your enemy is the one cut off﴾ was revealed, and ﴿Have you not seen those who were given a portion of the Scripture?﴾ [al-Nisaʾ: 44] down to His saying: ﴿then you will not find for him a helper﴾ [al-Nisaʾ: 52]." Ibn Kathir said: its chain is sound.

al-Ṭabarānī and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Abu Ayyub, who said: "When Ibrahim, the son of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), died, the polytheists walked among themselves and said: 'This *ṣābiʾ* has been cut off tonight.' So Allah revealed ﴿Indeed, We have given you al-Kawthar﴾ to the end of the surah."

Ibn Saʿd and Ibn ʿAsākir through the route of al-Kalbi, from Abu Ṣāliḥ, from Ibn ʿAbbas, said: "The eldest child of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was al-Qasim, then Zaynab, then ʿAbd Allah, then Umm Kulthum, then Fatimah, then Ruqayyah. al-Qasim died, and he was the first of his family and children to die in Mecca. Then ʿAbd Allah died. al-ʿĀṣ ibn Wāʾil al-Sahmi said: 'His line has been cut off, so he is *abtar*.' So Allah revealed ﴿Indeed, your enemy is the one cut off﴾." In its chain is al-Kalbi.

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Ḥātim and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn ʿAbbas concerning ﴿Indeed, your enemy is the one cut off﴾, that he said: "Abu Jahl."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Ḥātim reported from him concerning ﴿Indeed, your enemy﴾, that he said: "Your foe."

Abu al-Shaykh and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan reported from Anas, from the Prophet (ﷺ), something similar.

Ibn Abi Ḥātim, Ibn Shāhīn in his Sunan, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi reported from Ibn ʿAbbas concerning ﴿So pray to your Lord and sacrifice﴾, that he said: "When you pray and raise your head from bowing, stand upright."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 108, verses 1–3:

It is Meccan according to Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Kalbi and Muqatil, and Medinan according to al-Hasan, ʿIkrimah, Mujahid and Qatadah.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn al-Zubayr and ʿAʾishah that the surah of al-Kawthar was revealed in Mecca.

In the name of Allah, the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful.

The majority of readers recite ﴿Innā aʿṭaynāka﴾ (﴿Indeed, We have given you﴾). al-Hasan, Ibn Muḥaysin, Ṭalḥah and al-Zaʿfarānī read ﴿Anṭaynāka﴾ with an *nūn* (﴿Indeed, We have given you﴾, with the verb written with the letter *nūn*).

It is said that this is the dialect of the pure Arabs (*al-ʿarabiyyah al-ʿāribah*).

al-Aʿshā said:

*"Your gifts are the finest gifts of kings; you protect what is lawful and give away the unlawful."*

The word ﴿al-Kawthar﴾ is of the pattern *fawʿal*, derived from *al-kathrah* (abundance). It is used as an attribute to express intensity in abundance, like *al-nawfal* from *al-nafl* and *al-jawhar* from *al-jahr*.

The Arabs call everything abundant in number, quantity or worth *kawthar*. From this is the saying of the poet:

*"The dust of death has risen until it has become abundant."*

According to this, the meaning is: Indeed, We have given you, O Muhammad, abundant good that has reached the utmost extent of abundance.

Most of the exegetes, as al-Wahidi reported, held that al-Kawthar is a river in Paradise. It is also said that it is the Pool (*ḥawḍ*) of the Prophet (ﷺ) on the Standing Place (on the Day of Judgment). This was said by ʿAṭāʾ.

ʿIkrimah said: al-Kawthar is prophethood.

al-Hasan said: it is the Qur'an.

al-Hasan ibn al-Fadl said: it is the interpretation of the Qur'an and the lightening of the laws.

Abu Bakr ibn ʿAyyash said: it is the great number of companions and of the community (*ummah*).

Ibn Kaysan said: it is generosity (*al-īthār*).

It is also said that it is Islam, that it is the elevation of mention, that it is the light of the heart, that it is intercession, that it is miracles, that it is the answering of supplication, that it is "There is no god but Allah," that it is understanding of the religion, and that it is the five daily prayers. The correct view will be explained later.

﴿So pray to your Lord﴾. The *fāʾ* indicates that what follows is a consequence of what precedes. The intended meaning is a command to him (ﷺ) to persist in establishing the obligatory prayers. ﴿And sacrifice﴾ the camels, which were the best of the wealth of the Arabs.

Muhammad ibn Kaʿb said: some people used to pray to other than Allah and sacrifice to other than Allah, so Allah commanded His Prophet (ﷺ) that his prayer and his sacrifice be for Him alone.

Qatadah, ʿAṭāʾ and ʿIkrimah said: the intended meaning is the ʿEid prayer and the sacrifice of the Udhiyah (festival sacrifice).

It was said regarding *al-naḥr* (sacrifice, or the chest): placing the right hand upon the left during prayer, opposite the chest (*naḥr*). This was said by Muhammad ibn Kaʿb.

It is also said: it is raising the hands in prayer at the takbir up to the level opposite the chest.

It is also said: it is facing the qiblah with one's chest. This was said by al-Farrāʾ, al-Kalbi and Abu al-Aḥwas.

al-Farrāʾ said: I heard some Arabs say *nataḥāwar*, meaning *natagābal* (we face one another): the chest of this one facing the chest of that one, i.e., opposite it. From this is the saying of the poet:

*"O Abu Ḥakam, you are not a man of contention in your life, and the master of the people of al-Abṭaḥ is the one who faces (others)."*

That is, *al-mutaḥāwir* means the one who faces (another).

Ibn al-Aʿrabi said: it is a man standing in prayer facing the *miḥrāb*, from their saying: "Their dwellings face one another (*tatanāḥar*)," meaning they face one another.

It is reported from ʿAṭāʾ that he said: He was commanded to sit upright between the two prostrations until his chest is visible.

Sulayman al-Taymi said: the meaning is: raise your hands in supplication to your chest. The apparent meaning of the verse is a command to him (ﷺ) concerning prayer in general and sacrifice in general, and that he should make both of them for Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and not for anyone else. (p-1660) What the Sunnah has stated as an explanation of this general command, by a specific type, is in the status of a restriction of it, and it will come, Allah willing.

﴿Indeed, your enemy is the one cut off﴾. That is: indeed, your hater is the one cut off from good in general, so that it includes the good of this world and the Hereafter. Or it means: the one who has no offspring. Or: the one whose mention does not remain after his death.

The apparent meaning of the verse is general, and that this is the condition of everyone who hates the Prophet (ﷺ). That the cause of revelation was al-ʿĀs ibn Wāʾil does not contradict this, since what is considered is the generality of the wording, not the specificity of the cause, as has been mentioned before.

It was said: When the males among a man's children died, the people of the Jahiliyyah would say: "So-and-so has been cut off (*buttira*)." When the son of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), Ibrahim, died, Abu Jahl went out to his companions and said: "Muhammad has been cut off," so the verse was revealed. It is also said that the one who said this was ʿUqbah ibn Abi Muʿayṭ. The lexicographers said: *al-abtar* among men is the one who has no son; among animals, the one who has no tail; and every matter whose good effect has been cut off is *abtar*. The root *al-batr* means cutting. It is said: *batartu al-shay batran*, I cut the thing.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ahmad, Abu Dawud, al-Nasaʾi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan reported from Anas, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) dozed off briefly, then he raised his head smiling and said: 'Indeed, a surah was just revealed to me.' Then he recited ﴿Indeed, We have given you al-Kawthar﴾ until he finished it. Then he said: 'Do you know what al-Kawthar is?' They said: 'Allah and His Messenger know best.' He said: 'It is a river which my Lord has given me in Paradise, upon which is abundant good. My community will come to it on the Day of Resurrection. Its vessels are as numerous as the stars. A servant of them will be pulled back, and I will say: "O Lord, he is from my community," and it will be said: "You do not know what he innovated after you."'"

Muslim also reported it in his Ṣaḥīḥ.

al-Bukhari, Muslim and others reported from Anas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "I entered Paradise, and behold, there was a river whose two banks were tents of pearls. I struck with my hand at what the water flows through, and behold, it was musk, extremely fragrant. I said: 'What is this, O Jibril?' He said: 'This is al-Kawthar which Allah has given you.'" It has been reported from Anas through several chains, all of which explicitly state that al-Kawthar is the river that is in Paradise.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, al-Bukhari, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh reported from ʿAʾishah that she was asked about His saying: ﴿Indeed, We have given you al-Kawthar﴾, and she said: "It is a river which was given to your Prophet (ﷺ) in the innermost parts of Paradise (*buṭnān al-jannah*)."

Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn ʿAbbas that it is a river in Paradise.

al-Ṭabarānī in al-Awsaṭ reported from Ḥudhayfah concerning His saying: ﴿Indeed, We have given you al-Kawthar﴾, that he said: "A river in Paradise." al-Suyuti graded its chain as *ḥasan* (good).

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Usamah ibn Zayd, traced back to the Prophet (ﷺ) (*marfūʿan*): "It was said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): 'You have been given a river in Paradise called al-Kawthar.' He said: 'Yes, and its earth is ruby, coral, emerald and pearl.'"

Ibn Mardawayh reported from ʿAmr ibn Shuʿayb, from his father, from his grandfather, that "a man said: 'O Messenger of Allah, what is al-Kawthar?' He said: 'It is a river from the rivers of Paradise which Allah has given me.'" These ḥadīths indicate that al-Kawthar is the river in Paradise, so it is necessary to adopt this and not rely on other explanations. And although the linguistic meaning of al-Kawthar is abundant good in the language of the Arabs, whoever interprets it with something more general than what has been established from the Prophet (ﷺ) is giving an interpretation that looks to the linguistic meaning.

Likewise, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi, who graded it sound (*ṣaḥḥaḥahu*), Ibn Majah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh reported from ʿAṭāʾ ibn al-Sāʾib, who said: Muhārib ibn Dithār said: Saʿid ibn Jubayr said concerning al-Kawthar: "I said: 'Tell us from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said it is the abundant good.' He said: 'He spoke truly, indeed it is abundant good. But Ibn ʿUmar told us that when ﴿Indeed, We have given you al-Kawthar﴾ was revealed, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "al-Kawthar is a river in Paradise, its two banks are of gold, it flows over pearls and rubies, its soil is more fragrant than musk, its water is whiter than milk and sweeter than honey."'"

al-Bukhari, Ibn Jarir and al-Ḥākim, through the route of Abu Bishr from Saʿid ibn Jubayr, from Ibn ʿAbbas, reported that he said concerning al-Kawthar: "It is the good which Allah gave him."

Abu Bishr said: I said to Saʿid ibn Jubayr: "Indeed, some people claim that it is a river in Paradise." He said: "The river that is in Paradise is part of the good which Allah gave him."

This tafsir from the scholar of the Ummah, Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him, looks to the linguistic meaning as we have made known. But the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) has explained it, in what is authentically reported from him, as the river that is in Paradise. And when Allah's river comes, the river of Maʿqil is void.

Ibn Abi Ḥātim, al-Ḥākim, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan reported from ʿAli ibn Abi Ṭalib, who said: "When this surah was revealed upon the Prophet (ﷺ), ﴿Indeed, We have given you al-Kawthar﴾, ﴿So pray to your Lord and sacrifice﴾, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to Jibril: 'What is this *naḥīrah* (sacrifice) which my Lord has commanded me with?' He said: 'It is not a *naḥīrah*, but it commands you, when you begin the prayer with the takbir, to raise your hands when you say the takbir, when you bow, and when you raise your head from bowing. For it is our prayer and the prayer of the angels who are in the seven heavens. Indeed, every thing has an adornment, and the adornment of prayer is raising the hands at every takbir.' The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Raising the hands is from the humbling (*istikānah*) about which Allah said: ﴿So they did not humble themselves before their Lord, nor do they supplicate﴾ [al-Muʾminun: 76].'"
